hook.support: You’ve been in a group where two people do all the talking. Everyone else gives up. Nothing gets decided. A good leader fixes that. That leader can be you.
hook.core: You’ve been in that group: two people do all the talking, the rest switch off, and nothing gets decided. A good discussion leader changes everything. They open it up, keep it fair, and wrap it up. That leader can be you.
hook.extend: Every team meeting, group project and club committee has the same problem: a couple of voices dominate, the rest go quiet, and the group decides less well than it could. A good discussion leader fixes that. It isn’t about being the loudest. It’s about running the room so everyone’s thinking gets used.

why.support: Leading a group is a job skill. Team leaders, coaches and supervisors do it every day.
why.core: Running a discussion is a real job skill. Team leaders, shift supervisors, coaches and youth leaders do it every week. Research shows groups make better decisions when everyone gets a fair share of the talking.
why.extend: Facilitation is a core workplace skill: supervisors run toolbox talks, team leaders run meetings, and community groups run forums. Research shows that groups where the talking is shared make better decisions than groups dominated by one or two voices.

articles.title: Five moves to run the room

body.support:
A discussion leader doesn’t talk the most. They help **everyone** have a say. Use five moves.

1. **Open it.** Say the question. Say why it matters. Give two rules, like “one person talks at a time”.
2. **Go round.** Everyone says one thing first. Nobody speaks twice until all have spoken once.
3. **Dig in.** Ask follow-ups. “What makes you think that?” “Who sees it differently?”
4. **Keep it fair.** Bring in quiet people: “Mia, what do you think?” Stop talk-overs: “Hold on, let Sam finish.”
5. **Wrap it up.** Sum up what people said. Agree on a next step. Say thanks.

Your body helps too. Look around the whole group. Use an open hand to invite someone in. Keep your voice calm.
body.core:
A good discussion leader isn’t the person who talks the most. It’s the person who makes sure the **group** does its best thinking. You can do that with five moves.

1. **Open it.** Say the question clearly, say why it matters, and set two or three ground rules: “One person talks at a time. Disagree with the idea, not the person.” Say how long you have.
2. **Go round.** Give everyone a first turn before anyone speaks twice. It stops the loudest people taking over in the first minute.
3. **Dig in.** Respond to what people say. Ask for reasons and evidence: “What makes you think that?” Link ideas: “Building on what Jai said…” Bring out disagreement: “Who sees it differently?”
4. **Keep it fair.** Invite quieter people by name: “Ana, we haven’t heard from you yet.” Stop talk-overs politely: “Hold that thought, let Sam finish.” Pull people back on track: “Let’s get back to the question.”
5. **Wrap it up.** **Summarise** the main views fairly, including the ones you don’t agree with. Agree on a next step or a decision. Thank people.

Your body and voice do half the work. Stand or sit where you can see everyone. Sweep your eyes around the whole group. Use an open palm to hand someone the floor. Slow down when you summarise. A calm, steady voice keeps a heated discussion calm.
body.extend:
Leading a discussion is not about holding the floor. It’s about getting the best thinking out of the whole group. Experienced facilitators rely on five moves.

1. **Open it.** State the question precisely, explain why it matters and how long you have, and set two or three ground rules (“One voice at a time”, “Challenge ideas, not people”).
2. **Go round.** Give everyone an opening turn before anyone speaks twice. This prevents the first confident voices from framing the whole discussion.
3. **Dig in.** Respond to contributions rather than just collecting them. Probe for reasoning and evidence (“What makes you think that?”), connect ideas (“That links to Jai’s point about cost”) and surface disagreement (“Who sees it differently?”).
4. **Keep it fair.** Balance the airtime: invite quieter members by name, interrupt talk-overs respectfully, and redirect tangents. Fairness isn’t forcing everyone to talk equally; it’s making sure nobody is shut out.
5. **Wrap it up.** Summarise the range of views accurately, including those you disagree with, then steer towards a decision or next step. A fair summary is what makes people trust the outcome.

Your non-verbal leadership matters as much as your words. Position yourself to see everyone, distribute eye contact, use an open palm to hand over the floor, and slow your pace when summarising. When a discussion heats up, a lower, steadier voice signals calm and usually lowers the temperature.

caseStudies.title: The smartest groups share the talking

body.support:
In 2010, scientists in the United States tested **699** people. They put them in small groups of 2 to 5.

The groups did all kinds of tasks, like puzzles and plans.

The smartest groups were **not** the ones with the smartest people.

The best groups had two things:

- people who were good at **reading how others felt**
- talking that was **shared**, not taken over by one or two people

Groups where a few people did most of the talking did worse.
body.core:
In 2010, a team of scientists from universities in the United States wanted to know what makes some groups smarter than others. They tested **699** people, working in small groups of two to five, on all sorts of tasks: puzzles, planning and decisions.

They expected the smartest groups to be the ones with the smartest members. They were wrong. A group’s results were only loosely linked to how clever its members were.

The best groups had two things in common:

- members who were good at **reading other people’s feelings**, and
- **turn-taking**: the talking was spread around, not grabbed by one or two people.

Groups where a few people dominated the conversation did worse. The study was published in the journal *Science*.
body.extend:
In 2010, researchers from three American universities published a study in *Science*. Their question was simple. Is a group smart in its own way, apart from how smart its members are?

They tested **699** people in groups of two to five, on a wide range of tasks. Groups that did well on one task tended to do well on others. The team called this “collective intelligence”.

Surprisingly, it was only loosely linked to how clever the members were. It was more closely linked to two things. One was **social sensitivity**: how well members read each other’s feelings. The other was **equal turn-taking**. Groups where a few people dominated the talk scored lower.

For a discussion leader, the lesson is practical. Sharing out the talking isn’t just polite. It can make the group’s decisions better.

source.name: Woolley, Chabris, Pentland, Hashmi & Malone (2010), “Evidence for a collective intelligence factor in the performance of human groups”, Science (PubMed record)

model.text:
**Opening**

“Thanks for coming. Today’s question is: should our footy club start a girls’ team? We’ve got 10 minutes.

Two rules. One person talks at a time. And we challenge ideas, not people.

Let’s go round first. Yes, no or not sure, and one reason. Mia, can you start?”

**Wrap-up**

“Okay, let me sum up. Four of us said yes. The main reason was more players. Two said not yet. Their worry was finding a coach.

So the next step is to ask parents if anyone can coach. Jai will post that in the group chat by Friday. Thanks, everyone.”
why: The opening gives the question, the time and two rules before anyone argues.
Going round with “Mia, can you start?” stops the loudest people taking over.
The wrap-up sums up both sides fairly, then sets a clear next step: who, what and when.

teacher.overview: Students learn five discussion-leading moves (open, go round, dig in, keep it fair, wrap up) and the body language and voice that support them. They annotate a run sheet, plan their own, and lead a real 10-minute discussion with 4 to 6 people while an observer completes a talk tally. The case study is the 2010 Science study of 699 people which found groups with more equal turn-taking performed better.
prep: Print workbooks, plus spare talk-tally sheets for observers.
Prepare 6–8 safe, genuinely debatable questions (four-day week, phones at school, a local issue). Avoid topics that target identities.
Plan groups of 5–7 so each leader has 4–6 participants plus an observer; rotate leaders over two lessons.
Optional: a short clip of a well-run meeting or panel (e.g. a youth parliament committee).

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The moves
steps: **Hook (10 min):** run a deliberately bad 3-minute discussion (you let two students dominate). What went wrong?

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Why it matters + plan
steps: **Model (10 min):** lead a 5-minute discussion yourself, narrating your moves.
**Plan (25 min):** run sheets; practise opening lines in pairs.

lessons.title: Lessons 3–4 — Run the room
steps: **Discussions (60 min):** rotate leaders; observers complete talk tallies.
**Debrief (15 min):** look at tallies; what made it fair?
**Check & reflect (15 min):** quick check, reflection, sign-off.

keyPoints: The leader runs the room; they don’t take it over.
Open, go round, dig in, keep it fair, wrap up.
Groups decide better when the talking is shared.
Eyes around the group, open hand, calm pace.

support: Sentence starters and fair-play phrases on a card.
Lead a smaller group (3–4) for 6–8 minutes.
extend: Linking and probing questions; steer to a decision.

Uses appropriate body language and voice when presenting and summarising views.
Level Up: influences the group with a language device suited to them.

teacher.answers:
**Sort:** asking Ana — helps; only looks at best mate — hurts; hold that thought — helps; own opinion first for three minutes — hurts; fair summary — helps; drifting to the game — hurts.

**Annotation:** 1 open (question + time); 2 ground rules; 3 go round; 4 dig in (follow-ups); 5 keep it fair (invite + stop talk-over, with gesture); 6 wrap up (summary + next step, slow pace).

**Case study:** they expected the smartest members to make the smartest groups; instead, the best groups had socially sensitive members and shared turn-taking; groups dominated by a few did worse.

realityCheck: **Group composition makes or breaks this.** Put at least one cooperative student in each group, and don’t give the hardest group to your most anxious leader.
**Rotating leaders takes time.** With 25 students, plan two lessons of discussions, or let some students lead outside class (the solo option).
**Choose topics carefully.** Debatable but safe: timetables, phones, local projects. Avoid anything that puts a student’s identity up for debate.
**Eye contact and turn-taking norms vary across cultures**, including for some First Nations students. Frame the moves as tools for this setting, not rules about right and wrong.
**Works in a real class:** yes, and the talk tally makes progress visible. Students are often surprised by who did the talking.
